newsitem.title: USA: US - Asia "open skies" treaties to develop slowly.
newsitem.headline: US - Asia "open skies" treaties to develop slowly.

text.p: Liberal "open skies" treaties between the United States and Asia will develop slowly since many political, cultural and economic hurdles remain, airline industry experts said Thursday.

Speaking at the sixth annual Phoenix International Aviation Symposium, airline experts said Asian countries must first liberalize aviation treaties within Asia before significant strides can be made in expanding open skies pacts between the U.S. and Asia.

"Until Asian countries have open skies agreements among themselves, they will not be able to go to open skies with the U.S. or Europe. They need to be comfortable with competition among themselves first," said Germal Singh Khera, manager of international relations at Malaysian Airline System Bhd.
Although the U.S. has open skies agreements with some Asian countries, including Singapore and Brunei, additional pacts will be forged more slowly.

Mathew Samuel, director of corporate affairs at Singapore Airlines Ltd, said he expects southeast Asian countries to pave the way towards open skies. The southeast Asian countries will likely adopt air treaties among themselves before the turn of the century, Samuel said.
China, however, will move very slowly towards liberal aviation treaties.
"China may take a long while to test the code-sharing waters," said Ulrich Schulte-Strathaus, vice president of international relations with Deutsche Lufthansa AG.
"China open skies, quite frankly, is very far down the road. You first have to get the aviation industry in China settled before it can branch out," Samuel said.

The cost structure of many Asian carriers is too high to make them viable partners with U.S. airlines. Until Asian carriers can cut costs and improve operating efficiencies, they would be a drain on many potential alliance partners, industry executives said.
Lufthansa, for example, spent years restructuring and cutting costs before forging its alliance with UAL Corp's United Airlines, Schulte-Strathaus said.
A move towards privatization by some Asian airlines lays the ground-work for open skies.

"Those countries with a capitalist bent are more apt to do open skies. I don't think that trend will be any different in Asia. Privatization is the single biggest factor in bringing open skies to the agenda," Samuel said.
Some private companies are acquiring ownership stakes in some Asian national carriers, that had previously been supported by government subsidies.
"The idea that countries need a national carrier to fly the flag around while draining the nations' coffers is over," Samuel said.

Another obstacle to U.S.-Asian open skies treaties is infrastructure constraints. Several major Asian airports have limited extra room to give potential U.S. alliance partners slot spaces, hangar facilities or administrative office space.

"Before we can address open skies, we have to address infrastructure issues. I don't think any U.S. carrier could get any slots in Tokyo because there's none available. Even if an open skies agreement was signed, it would only be a paper agreement, not a working agreement, since there's no room there," Khera said.
While many industry experts said Asian-U.S. open skies treaties would be slow to develop, Richard Hirst, senior vice president of corporate affairs for Northwest Airlines Corp, was more optimistic.

Citing the success of several air treaties between the U.S. and Europe, Hirst said "there is no reason why that model would not be acceptible to Asian countries. I believe that template fits and I believe we'll see moves to Asia happening more quickly than many think."
